Note: Preferred template (survives editor review verbatim ~15x): 'Here the author/speaker is speaking as if X were Y. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use...' Keep this structure; do not over-explain.
Preferred template: 'The point of this comparison is that just as X, so is Y. If it would be helpful in your language, you could ...' Editors keep ~90% of simile notes in this form.
Preferred template: 'Here, **X** represents Y. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [...]' Editors keep ~87%.

Write only for genuinely abstract/theological ideas. Editors delete ~38% overall - especially notes on common nouns (tears, pain, life, violence, salvation, anger) and on repeated occurrences. Flag a given abstract noun once per passage, not every verse; later occurrences are covered by pipeline-generated see-how / also-occurs sentences.
Content-team mandate: every passive instance still gets a note - do not drop. Historical context only: editors deleted ~55% of these in LAM/HAB poetry before the mandate.
Only write when an antecedent is genuinely ambiguous across a clause boundary. Editors delete ~43%.
Skip for ordinary possessives; write only for non-ownership relations (e.g. 'daughter of Zion'). Editors delete ~61%.
Rarely worth a note in poetry; editors delete ~78%.
Only when the rhetorical force is not obvious to a modern reader. Editors delete ~42%.
Apply a high bar - editors delete ~50%; only supply implicit info a translator could not infer.
Genre-dependent: editors deleted 57% in HAB but kept all in LAM. Write only when the parallel line adds meaning, not for every poetic couplet.

Expand name notes beyond bare identification ('The word X is the name of a man/place'). When the name carries cultural or narrative significance, include that context: character role (e.g. 'the Babylonian name of Daniel'), corrected spelling (e.g. 'Azal' not 'Azel'), or meaning/function (e.g. 'Qoheleth is a title meaning one who assembles a group'). Drop minimal bare-identification notes for undistinguished persons in genealogical lists — editors removed all such notes in 1CH:2 and MIC:1.
Context: name notes: add cultural context; drop bare identification in genealogical lists

Note: Add a note when embedded speech begins inside a verse without an explicit quotation-introduction verb or marker, particularly in visionary and narrative prose. Template: 'This is the beginning of what [speaker] told [listener]. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could introduce this as a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [He told me, \'These great beasts\']'. Also note double-verb introductions ('answered and said') that natural-language translations may simplify: 'The terms answered and said together introduce a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent both terms.'
Context: embedded speech without explicit marker; double-verb quotation introductions

Note: Add a note when: (1) a verse has ambiguous structural attachment and could belong to either the preceding or following section — list both options as numbered alternatives: 'This verse could go with: (1) the previous section ([ref]). See the ULT and UST. (2) the following section ([ref])'; (2) the clause or information order is unusual and translators may need to reorder — template: 'You could put [X] before [Y]. The UST models one way to do that.' Use figs-infostructure for ordering issues only when the displacement is significant enough that a translator might otherwise misread the sequence.
Context: structural attachment ambiguity; unusual clause order

Note: Drop a figs-idiom note when a figs-metaphor note in the same verse already addresses the same phrase — editors removed idiom notes for 'loosening of knots' and 'make themselves hear' when metaphor notes covered the same ground. When keeping an idiom note, provide two alternate translations: one that paraphrases the idiom closely and one that states the meaning plainly (e.g. '[Belshazzar became drunk and said] or [while under the influence of the wine]'). Single-AT idiom notes are consistently revised to dual-AT form.
Context: drop when redundant with adjacent figs-metaphor; always provide dual alternate translations

Note: When writing a symbolic action note, always include: (1) what the action communicates culturally, (2) an offer to explain in text or footnote. For compact investiture gestures (robes, chains, status markers), a brief form suffices: 'These were symbols of [rank/authority]. Alternate translation: [verb phrase showing the significance]'. For ritual actions with theological weight (drinking from sacred vessels, mocking a deity), provide fuller explanation of what the action communicated to the original audience and why it was significant.
Context: note content structure: brief for investiture, fuller for ritual/theological actions

Note: In Daniel's Aramaic chapters, the particle כְּעַן ('now') and וּכְעַן ('and now') function as discourse-attention markers that focus the audience on the speaker's main or concluding point. Add a writing-foreground note when the particle introduces the climactic statement in a speech. Template: '[Speaker] is using the term **Now** (or **And now**) to focus [listener's] attention on what [he/she] is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [So] or [And so]'. Distinguish from hinneh (behold) notes which follow the existing ALL-book template.
Context: Aramaic ke'an / uke'an as speech-climax discourse marker
